title: Megaways Slots Explained for Canadian Players 2026
excerpt: How the Megaways engine really works, why 117,649 ways to win does not mean better odds, and the one thing Canadian players should check before spinning.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Open the slot lobby at almost any Canadian casino site and the word appears within seconds. Megaways slots take up a large share of the shelf space in this market, and the badge now sits on games from dozens of studios, not one developer. What it describes is not a theme but a piece of engineering: a licensed reel-modifier engine, originally built by the Australian studio Big Time Gaming and licensed out to other providers, which changes how many symbols each reel displays on every spin. The number attached to the standard version is 117,649 ways to win. That figure is arithmetic rather than marketing, and it tells you almost nothing about whether a given game is good value.

What the engine actually does

Reels that change height every spin

On a conventional slot the grid is fixed: five reels, three symbols each, the same shape on every spin. This engine removes that constraint. Each reel is fed from a larger symbol strip and stops with a variable number of positions showing, commonly two to seven on the standard six-reel layout. One spin might show a squat 3-2-4-2-3-2 grid, the next seven symbols on every reel. The number of winning combinations available is therefore different on every spin.

Where 117,649 comes from

The maximum is simple multiplication. Six reels, each capable of showing up to seven symbols, gives 7 to the sixth power, or 117,649. That is the ceiling, not the average; most spins land well below it, because all six reels rarely expand at once. Extended variants add a horizontal reel, a seventh reel, or more symbols per reel, pushing the theoretical maximum into the millions. A bigger headline number is a design choice, not evidence of a more generous game.

Ways to win are not paylines

A payline is a defined geometric path across the grid, and a symbol only counts if it lands on that exact path. Ways to win discard geometry entirely. A combination pays if matching symbols land on consecutive reels starting from the leftmost reel, regardless of which row each one occupies.

Two consequences follow. You cannot choose how many lines to play, because there are none; your stake covers all available ways as a single fixed bet. And the count of ways is a product of the reel heights, so it swings dramatically: a 2-2-2-2-2-2 spin offers 64 ways, a 7-7-7-7-7-7 spin offers 117,649. Our guide to online slots in Canada covers how this compares with fixed-payline and cluster-pays formats.

Cascades and the multiplier trail

Nearly every title also bundles in cascading reels, sold as tumbling or avalanche reels. When a combination forms, those symbols are removed, the ones above drop into the gaps, and new symbols fill in from the top. If the new arrangement creates another win, the process repeats, so a single paid spin can chain into several consecutive wins.

The free spins round is where the engine shows its hand. The common implementation attaches a win multiplier to the cascade sequence, and that multiplier does not reset between spins during the bonus, often with no stated upper limit: it climbs by one with every successful cascade and keeps climbing. That is why these games advertise enormous maximum wins, and why those wins are rare.

Why Megaways slots are inherently high-volatility

Volatility describes the shape of the returns, not their size: a low-volatility game pays small amounts often, a high-volatility game pays rarely and large. This architecture sits firmly at the second end, by design rather than accident. A very large slice of the game's expected return is allocated to the free spins round with its uncapped multiplier, and money committed there is money not paid out in the base game. So the base game runs cold by design, the bonus triggers infrequently, and most bonus rounds end modestly because the multiplier never got the cascades it needed. The distribution is spiky: long flat stretches interrupted occasionally by a result that looks nothing like the rest of the session. Budget on the assumption that the flat stretch is the normal experience.

The RTP problem: one game, several different numbers

This is the most important practical point here, and it applies to these titles more than most because so many are licensed builds distributed across many operators. Providers frequently ship the same game in multiple RTP configurations. A headline release might be marketed at somewhere around 96 percent, while lower-configured versions of the identical game, same graphics, same features, same name, are made available to operators at meaningfully reduced settings. Nothing on the screen changes; the only difference is the maths model the operator has licensed. A review or a video quoting an RTP figure is describing whichever version that writer saw, not what is running in front of you. The only reliable source is the game's own information screen at the casino you are playing at, usually reached through the paytable or rules button inside the game window.

Feature buys and the Ontario question

Many of these games include a feature buy, sometimes called a bonus buy: pay a fixed multiple of your stake, often in the range of fifty to a hundred times, and enter the free spins round without waiting for a natural trigger. It is usually priced close to the game's ordinary return and does not manufacture value. What it does is compress volatility into one transaction, resolving in under a minute what would otherwise take a few hundred base spins.

Availability also differs across the Canadian market. In regulated Ontario play, feature buy mechanics are restricted, and players there will often find the button missing from games that carry it elsewhere. Our overview of Ontario casino apps sets out the wider differences between the two markets.

How the mechanic behaves on mobile

These games are demanding to render. Variable reel heights, cascade animations and multiplier trails mean the screen is constantly rebuilding itself, and on a phone a seven-symbol reel can become hard to read. Better builds use a redesigned portrait layout rather than a shrunk desktop one, and let you switch animations off. Check that the RTP information button is reachable, since it is often buried in a menu on mobile. Practical stake sizing

The volatility profile has direct implications for bet size.

  • Bet smaller than you would on a low-volatility game. A per-spin stake well under one percent of your session budget is a sensible starting point.
  • Expect the dry stretch. Several hundred spins without a bonus trigger is ordinary, not a sign that a game is due.
  • Set the session budget before you open the game. The urge to raise stakes after a cold run is strongest precisely when the maths says nothing has changed.
  • Treat feature buys as a separate budget line. One buy can equal a hundred base spins.
  • Check the RTP at each new casino. The configuration can differ between operators.

The honest summary

The engine is a genuinely clever piece of design, and it is entertaining in a way fixed-line slots are not. What it does not do is improve your expected return. It redistributes the same house edge into a spikier shape: fewer, rarer, larger wins funded by longer stretches of nothing. A 117,649-way game is not more generous than a 25-line game with the same RTP, only more dramatic.
